title: Gamaliel's advice (Acts 5:12–42)
hook: if it's from God, you won't be able to stop it
tomorrow: the church grows, and some widows get missed at dinner. who notices?

segments.voice: Yesterday's hard story drew a clear line: give what you give, no pretending. Today the apostles are back in front of the council.

Some group chats have one person who says, let's wait a day, while everyone else is furious. Acts 5 has that person. The apostles stand before the council again, and Peter's answer is short: "We ought to obey God rather than men." The room is enraged; Acts says they took counsel to slay them. Then one man stands up: "a Pharisee, named Gamaliel, a doctor of the law, had in reputation among all the people." And what he says is: let them alone.
screen: `THE ONE WHO SAYS, WAIT A DAY.` → `OBEY GOD RATHER THAN MEN.` → `GAMALIEL STANDS UP.`

segments.voice: He has the apostles put outside for a little while and speaks to the council. Take care, he says, what you mean to do. He reminds them of movements that rose before, Theudas and Judas of Galilee; each gathered followers, and each came to nothing. Then his advice: "Refrain from these men, and let them alone: for if this counsel or this work be of men, it will come to nought: But if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it; lest haply ye be found even to fight against God." Notice who the calm voice is: a Pharisee, a teacher of the law, honored by the people. The council takes his advice, partly. They still have the apostles beaten and order them not to speak in Jesus' name, then let them go. And the apostles leave "rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for his name." Gamaliel's test is patient. It isn't indifference; he warns about fighting against God. It isn't approval either; Acts never says he joined them. It's humility about how much one angry room can know in one afternoon. One to tell a friend tonight: later in Acts, Paul says he was brought up "at the feet of Gamaliel." The teacher who said wait had a student who would turn the whole story.
screen: `MOVEMENTS THAT CAME TO NOTHING.` · `REFRAIN, AND LET THEM ALONE.` · `A PHARISEE, THE CALM VOICE.` · `AT THE FEET OF GAMALIEL.` · then, large: `IF IT BE OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Stand and walk slowly, a few steps and back, for about a minute. With each step, hold one thing you're ready to oppose: a plan, an idea, someone's suggestion. Don't decide; let the steps give it time, then sit and breathe with whatever is left.
Gamaliel's advice. Let them alone: if it's only human, it will fade; if it's from God, you can't stop it.
Your line: if it be of God, time will show it, so wait and see. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1496 COUNTS.` → `ACTS, READ THROUGH · 10 OF 45.` → `TOMORROW: THE CHURCH GROWS, AND SOME WIDOWS GET MISSED AT DINNER. WHO NOTICES?`

howItsDone: Some Christians quote Gamaliel's 'if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it' when a new idea or movement divides a congregation, as a reason to wait before opposing it.

fork.setup: a new hire at work suggests a whole new way to run the weekly meeting. your gut says it won't work. what's Gamaliel's way?

fork.reveal: if this counsel be of men, it will come to nought: but if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it. Gamaliel trusted time to sort it.

chat.says: the English class families want to add their own song at the end. it'll run long. Pop says wait. ugh
options: Pop's right: hear them out before saying no. Gamaliel said wait and see.
Say no now. Gamaliel told the council to stop it before it spread.

chat.meaning: Gamaliel said refrain and let them alone; time shows what's of God. Waiting before opposing isn't approval. It's humility.

notes: Gamaliel, a Pharisee, is presented as the calm, respected voice the text describes (Acts 5:34), never as a foil; a myth item corrects the popular idea that Pharisees are always villains. Acts 5:28 and 5:30 ('whom ye slew') are left out on purpose.
Theudas and Judas of Galilee (Acts 5:36–37) are named without numbers or dates; the historical questions about Theudas are left out under the claims rule.
'Acts never says he joined them' stays with the text; later Christian legends about Gamaliel are left out.

Acts 22:3 ('at the feet of Gamaliel') is quoted ahead of the read-through as the day's fact to tell a friend; 'a student who would turn the whole story' anticipates Paul without teaching his story. Confirm.
The beating (5:40) is mentioned briefly and plainly. The earlier part of the chapter (signs, Peter's shadow, the prison doors opened, 5:12–25) is cut for length.
